1:
Paul opens by asserting a commission, and every voice reads the assertion as defensive. Ellicott says his authority was questioned at Corinth; Henry adds that asserting it was proper at any time but necessary at this time, and was not pride but faithfulness to a trust. Robertson takes the word as a verbal adjective with no verb to be, so that it reads a called apostle — not so-called, but one whose apostleship is due neither to himself nor to men. Wesley finds two exclusions: by the mention of God the authority of man, by the will of God the merit of Paul. Clarke reports a proposal to repunctuate, a comma after the participle giving Paul the called, the apostle of Jesus Christ — the first signifying called to, the second sent from. Chrysostom makes the one word a rebuke before any argument begins: Paul was called while persecuting the Church, so that of him who calls is everything and of him who is called nothing but to obey.

The two names draw out two antiquarians. Gill notes that a Jew born in a Roman city might carry two names. John Lightfoot documents the custom: either the same name turned into the other tongue, as Tabitha is Dorcas, or a different one, as Herod is Agrippa. On the companion Ellicott identifies him with the ruler of the synagogue beaten before the judgment-seat and conjectures he was the amanuensis. Barnes marks what is not known — when he was converted, or why he was now at Ephesus — and insists he was neither apostle nor inspired. Wesley reads the title as emphatic, that from a Jewish opposer he became a faithful brother.

That such a body could be called the church of God is the hard question. Robertson settles it grammatically, the genitive showing it belongs to God and not to any faction, and notes the city was now very rich and very corrupt, its name a byword for vile immorality. Ellicott makes it a protest against party spirit — the Church of God, not of this or that man. Gill calls it a very high character given to a people among whom were many disorders, which shows a church is not unchurched for everything amiss in it. Calvin presses hardest: it may seem strange to name a multitude so infested with distempers that Satan might be said to reign among them rather than God, and he answers from the promise that God had much people there, and from the tokens still remaining. He turns it into a warning that whoever requires a Church without wrinkle or stain must end by withdrawing from everyone and reckoning himself the only saint in the world, or founding a sect with a few hypocrites.

Barnes denies that sanctified refers to profession, holding they were in fact holy, and that the calling was not a mere invitation but was made effectual. John Lightfoot divides where Barnes will not, subdividing the phrase into those truly saints and those saints by profession. Ellicott refuses the modern restriction, the term being applied to the whole baptised body, the nearest English being simply Christians. Clarke reads it as separation from the corruptions of their place and age, and takes the address to all in every place as proof the letter was meant for the universal Church; Barnes draws the same inference and adds that calling on the name implies worship, which Wesley states plainly, that all Christians pray to Christ. Cyril of Jerusalem argues that since man is of twofold nature the cleansing is twofold, the water cleansing the body and the Spirit sealing the soul. On the greeting five of them send the reader elsewhere, Calvin saying he does not willingly burden his readers with repetitions; only Tertullian lingers, noting that what the apostle prescribes is not the usual health but grace and peace.
4:
Five voices read the thanksgiving as tactics, and say so. Barnes notes that before stating the disorders the apostle commends them for attainments they had really made, and adds that commending accords with the gospel as much as reproving — a minister, or a parent, may do as much good by judicious commendation. Ellicott says they secure attention at the outset and show he is not blind to their good qualities nor about to utter words of hopeless condemnation but of wholesome warning. Calvin, having said the salutation secured authority, says this procures favour, soothing their minds that they may listen patiently to the reproofs, and cites Theodoret: being about to censure, he soothes the organ of hearing so the remedy may be received. Wesley observes that congratulating them on the gifts they most admired tended to soften their spirits and make way for what follows. Chrysostom alone grounds it theologically: what Paul exhorts others to do he does himself in almost every epistle, and the occasion is more urgent here, because whoever gives thanks acknowledges a favour — and a favour is not a debt, nor a requital, nor a payment, worth saying to men gaping after the dividers of the Church.

The possessive and the singular both draw comment. Chrysostom says that out of great affection he seizes on what is common and makes it his own; Gill takes it as expressing his faith of interest, and as reminding them that all they enjoyed came from one who was his God and theirs. Ellicott reads the emphatic singular, against the plural just before, as showing that Paul writes in his own name and on his sole authority. Robertson points out that even at Corinth he finds something to thank God for, though the second epistle has none at all because of the acute crisis, and neither has Galatians; here he lets his general attitude override the specific causes of irritation.

What they were enriched in divides them. Clarke insists the first word should certainly be translated doctrine, all the truths of God relative to their salvation having been explicitly declared and perfectly comprehended. Ellicott makes it faculty, not content — the power of outward expression. John Lightfoot identifies the pair with tongues and prophesying. Robertson takes them as the unusual spiritual gifts which were their glory and became their peril, and dwells on the verb, an old causative that dropped out for centuries and reappeared in the Greek Old Testament, used in the New Testament by Paul alone. Gill fills the riches out as the riches of grace and Christ's own unsearchable riches, coming through his poverty. Barnes reads the word as marking both abundance and value, a treasure properly so called.

How the testimony was confirmed is the second dispute, and Calvin stages it. Erasmus, he reports, rendered the clause the other way round; Calvin says the words are easy if not wrested — God sealed the truth of his gospel among them to confirm it — and then asks by what means. Chrysostom, he says, seems to understand it of miracles; he takes it more largely, since the gospel is properly confirmed in our experience by faith, when we set to our seal that God is true. Gill will not choose, listing the miracles that attended the preaching, the extraordinary gifts, and the inward power of the Spirit. Barnes stays with the gifts and makes them a continued miracle, demonstrating the gospel in the same measure as at the first. Robertson calls the genitive objective and notes the verb means to make stand, the gifts having been given for that purpose. Ellicott has it both ways at once, the testimony Paul bore to Christ and from Christ. Wesley draws the pastoral point: they knew they had received these gifts by the hand of Paul, and remembering it would revive their reverence for their spiritual father.
7:
The commendation is qualified two ways. Ellicott points out that the clause is comparative — they come behind others in no gift. Barnes widens the noun, denying it refers necessarily to miraculous endowments and taking it to include all the kindnesses of God in producing peace of mind, constancy and humility; Gill says the same more briefly, ordinary or extraordinary. Calvin works the verb, which means to come too late for a thing and so miss it, quoting Xenophon on Abrocomas coming too late for the battle. Robertson calls it a wonderful record — then undercuts it, noting that in the second epistle Paul must complain they had not paid their pledges for the collection, made over a year before, a very modern complaint.

What they were waiting for is Clarke's difficulty alone. He finds it hard to say whether the apostle means the final judgment or the Lord's coming to destroy Jerusalem and end the Jewish polity, and since Paul does not explain himself he must mean something the readers knew well; at the next verse he lays the two readings side by side again. Everyone else takes the second coming without hesitation. Ellicott calls it the second visible appearance, which the early Church expected would soon occur, awaited neither with fear nor impatience but with calm trustfulness. Wesley makes the posture diagnostic: to long for this revelation, or to dread it, is a sure mark of a true or a false Christian.

Who it is that shall confirm them splits the grammarians from each other. Robertson says flatly that the relative points to Christ. Calvin says it refers not to Christ but to God, though God is the remoter antecedent, the apostle being still at his congratulation and now telling them what hope he has of them. Gill argues it out: Christ is the nearer antecedent, but the confirmation is made in him, and the end in view is blamelessness in his day, so the confirmer must be the Father, to whom the thanksgiving has run all along. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion, resting it on the general sense rather than on the wording of the phrase. Robertson glosses the closing adjective as unimpeachable, since none will have the right to impeach.

Whether the keeping is unconditional divides the same men again. Barnes takes it as one of the many places expressing Paul's confidence that true Christians shall be preserved and not suffered to fall away. Clarke makes it turn on conduct — as the testimony was confirmed among them, so in conscientiously believing and obeying God will confirm them — and Wesley writes the condition into the verse itself, who will confirm you if you faithfully apply to him, adding that now it is our day, wherein we work out our salvation. The ground they all appeal to is the same. Gill argues from God's faithfulness to his promises and from effectual calling, since whom he calls he also glorifies; Barnes rests the evidence of their persevering on the fidelity of God. Calvin puts it bluntly: God is steadfast in what he purposes, and does not make sport as to his calling — the calling of each of his own is not mere play, and in calling them he does not mock them. Robertson traces the last word through partnership, participation, intimacy, and even the contribution of money. Clarke reports that the faithfulness of God was a favourite expression among the ancient Jews for his integrity in preserving what is entrusted to him, and tells their story of the rabbi who for seven years sowed and reaped barley two men had forgotten with him, then bade them take their treasure. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the title on the reader: since God is called Faithful, the catechumen transferred into the order of the Faithful receives a great dignity in that name, becoming partaker of a title of God.
10:
The manner of the appeal is noticed before its matter. Chrysostom takes it as a lesson in method: rebukes must be framed gently and gradually, and Paul, entering on a subject enough to tear up the Church from her foundations, beseeches, and beseeches through Christ, taking Christ to fight on his side and aid his injured Name. Sharp rebuke at once, he adds, makes a man fierce and impudent, but shame bows down his neck. Calvin has the same instinct in another figure, a skilful surgeon soothing the wound before applying a painful remedy. Gill notes that Paul does not lay his commands on them, which he might have done, but entreats, styling them brethren. Robertson glosses the verb as calling to one's side, the name being the medium of the appeal rather than its cause.

What unity is asked for is defined downward. Clarke allows that if they did not agree in opinion on every subject they might still agree in the words expressing their faith, and asks why communion need be interrupted when all genuine Christians agree on essentials. Henry qualifies twice: in the great things of religion be of a mind, and be joined together as far as you can. Wesley reduces the second term to alienation of affection and challenges anyone to find the word taken in another sense in Scripture. Ellicott insists on what the factions were not — not sects separated from the Church but parties within it, each named after some favoured apostle. Robertson finds the phrase an idiom of Greek political life, evidence of Paul's acquaintance with Greek culture. Barnes locates the cause in philosophy, ambition for distinction, and the exhibition of popular eloquence among the Corinthian teachers.

The informants are named, and nobody agrees who they were. Clarke makes Chloe a religious matron at Corinth whose sons were the three men named at the close of the epistle; Wesley has heard her supposed the wife of one and mother of the other two. Ellicott says plainly that who she was we cannot tell, taking the messengers for slaves of her household travelling between the cities. Robertson notes the phrase about a household is not in the Greek, and that whether these were her children, kinspeople or servants is unknown, as is whether she lived in Corinth or Ephesus. Barnes adds that their own letter had not reported it. Gill says the evidence was so full they could not deny it; Calvin explains that general observations have little effect, so Paul shows they had not merely turned aside from holy unity but fallen into contentions, which are worse.

The four watchwords raise two questions. First, whether they are the real names: Barnes reports that many ancient interpreters supposed Paul was unwilling to name the actual leaders and substituted his own and his colleagues'; Calvin mentions the figure by which a writer repeats his opponents' own words. Second, what the last watchword means. Ellicott records the suggestion that it is not a fourth party but Paul's own counter-affirmation, and rejects it, since nothing in the expression marks a change of sense and there are traces elsewhere of such a party. John Lightfoot offers two explanations from the Jewish side: if any had received only the baptism of John, as some had at Ephesus, no wonder they said they were of the Messiah, not yet knowing Jesus to be he; or, many still inclining to Judaism may have meant that every man should be enrolled under the Messiah alone as Captain, under none deputed by him. Wesley says they spoke well, had they not on that pretence despised their teachers, and wonders whether they valued themselves on having heard Christ in person. Robertson observes that the man whose name was taken in vain refused to be a party to the strife, returned to Ephesus, and would not go back.
13:
Whether the first clause is a question at all is disputed. Ellicott reads it as a statement — Christ, in the communion of the Church, is rent and torn in fragments by you — the sacred name used as a party-cry making the apostle burst out. Gill reports both readings and answers no: the human body was not divided, a bone of it not broken, the seamless garment not rent, and the mystical body is not to be torn either. Robertson holds it probably interrogative, records that Hofmann called the assertory form a rhetorical impossibility, and observes that the missing negative particle merely allows an affirmative answer which is true. Calvin makes it true in a restricted way: since only a few retained Christ as Master while all boasted the Christian name, Christ was by this means torn asunder.

The two questions that follow are one argument. Clarke puts it bluntly: the gospel proclaims salvation through the crucified only, and Paul has not poured out his blood for them, so being called by his name is absurd. Barnes makes the same point structurally, Christ's claims arising from his crucifixion and acknowledged in their baptism; Wesley denies that Christ's glory is to be divided between him and his servants. Clarke adds that to be baptized into a name implied becoming that person's disciple. Robertson recalls that Jesus himself baptized no one, precisely to avoid this controversy, and denies outright that Paul can be claimed as a sacramentalist. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies what baptism was taken to be: the cleansing is twofold because man is, the water cleansing the body while the Spirit seals the soul.

The thanksgiving that follows embarrasses them. Henry states the difficulty rather than dodging it — how was this a proper matter for thankfulness, when baptizing all nations was part of the commission, and could Paul thank God for neglecting a duty? — and answers that he is not thankful for having baptized none at all. Gill guards it: not that Paul disliked the ordinance, but since some made an ill use of his having baptized them he was thankful it had been so ordered. Calvin turns it into a reproach, that their perversity made him avoid a thing so sacred; he would have acted rightly had he baptized ever so many, and rejoices only that providence ordered otherwise. Barnes puts the reason plainly, that he had given no occasion for the suspicion of setting himself up as head of a party. Wesley notes the phrase is a pious form of the common one, I rejoice.

The names draw out the antiquarians again. Ellicott suggests that the importance of the first two, and their being early converts, may explain why the apostle departed from his usual practice with them. Robertson identifies one as the former ruler of the synagogue and the other as probably the host of Paul and of the whole church, possibly the man addressed in John's third epistle. John Lightfoot presses that into a further conclusion: if that Gaius were the Corinthian, which he thinks very probable, then John seems to have written his first epistle to the Corinthians, since he writes to a particular church and one where Gaius resided — a chain Clarke reproduces and credits to him. The afterthought about the household is read the same way twice: Ellicott calls it a subsequent correction, the apostle having forgotten them and been reminded possibly by the man writing from his dictation, and Robertson reports the same suggestion. Gill thinks the head of that house the Philippian jailer, and denies that any argument for infant baptism can be formed from a household; Barnes will say only that whether there were infants does not appear. Clarke ends by defending the admission that he does not recollect, protesting at those who construe the doubt so as to affect his inspiration.
17:
Nobody lets the denial stand as it reads. Clarke adopts a rendering that makes it comparative — sent not so much to baptize as to preach — defended from the Hebrew idiom by which preference is expressed by affirming one thing and denying its contrary; otherwise Paul baptized without a commission. Gill reaches the same place by argument: he had the same mission the rest had, and had he not been sent to baptize it would have been unlawful for him to administer it at all. Calvin treats the clause as anticipating an objection, that he had not discharged his duty since Christ commands the apostles to baptize as well as teach, and answers that baptism is joined to teaching as an appendage, teaching holding the first place; he then guards the point twice, that the apostle does not absolutely deny a command to baptize, since he would have acted rashly in baptizing anyone without authority, and that nothing here detracts from the dignity of the sacrament. Robertson finds the qualification in the syntax, the negative attaching not to the infinitive but to the verb of sending: Christ did not send him to be a baptizer, as John was. Barnes notes the Saviour likewise did not personally baptize, and Wesley that all the apostles were sent to baptize too.

Why the work was left to others gets four different answers. Barnes gives the political one first — had the apostles baptized, those baptized by them might have claimed superiority and made parties — then a practical one, that baptism was probably attended by instruction better entrusted to those who stayed as teachers than to men travelling about. Calvin argues from scarcity and arithmetic: it was given to few to teach while many could baptize, and many could be taught at once while baptism is administered one by one, so Paul applied himself to the work more needful for him and left the rest to others. Ellicott and Robertson simply record the practice, that preaching was the apostles' work while deacons baptized. John Lightfoot answers from the mission field instead. Paul was not appointed a baptist among the Gentiles as John was among the Jews, and the offices were not alike: the Jews were instructed from their cradles in the doctrine of the Messiah, so John needed little pains to prepare them, whereas the Gentiles had never heard of Christ or of the true God, so Paul preached daily and instilled the doctrine drop by drop, it being no small labour to lead them leisurely to a baptizable measure.

On the manner of preaching they converge. Henry lists what is excluded — the enticing words of man's wisdom, the flourish of oratory, the accuracies of philosophical language on which the Greeks prided themselves, and which seem to have recommended the very men heading the faction against him — and adds that Paul, bred up at the feet of Gamaliel, laid his learning aside in preaching the cross. The truth, he says, needed no artificial dress but shone out in its own light, the plain preaching of a crucified Jesus proving more powerful than all the oratory and philosophy of the heathen world. Wesley calls the excluded thing the artificial ornaments of discourse invented by human wisdom, and states the risk exactly: the whole effect of the preaching was owing to the power of God accompanying a plain declaration that Christ bore our sins upon the cross, and might have been imputed to another cause had the preacher come with the wisdom of speech they admired. Henry puts the same danger the other way, that the success would be ascribed to the force of art and not of truth, and the honour of the cross be eclipsed. Ellicott adds the defensive point that this, and not inability or ignorance, was the grand cause of the apostle's simplicity.
18:
The phrase is defined negatively. Gill rules out the Christian's own cross, which he is to take up and bear, and keeps it to the cross of Christ — salvation by a crucified Christ, reconciliation by the blood of his cross. Barnes argues it harder: the statement that Christ died as a martyr cannot be what appears foolish, since the deaths of other martyrs excite admiration rather than contempt, so what offends must be the doctrine of atonement itself. Ellicott points out that the contrast is sharper in the original, the same word for speech being repeated — the word of the cross against the wisdom of words above — and that this is the word of real power. Robertson notes that by this incidental allusion the apostle passes to a new subject, the quarrels forgotten for a time while he corrects their exaltation of human eloquence.

The two classes are described in tenses that matter. Clarke divides the hearers into unbelievers and gainsayers who are perishing, and obedient believers in a state of salvation. Ellicott prefers the participles as continuous — those that are perishing, and us who are being saved — and Robertson makes the participle timeless, of those in the path to destruction, not annihilation. Wesley locates the cause in the will, perishing by obstinately rejecting the only saving name. Chrysostom supplies the picture: to the sick and gasping even wholesome meats are unpleasant and friends burdensome, often accounted intruders, and so with those perishing in soul, who do not know what tends to salvation and think those who care for them troublesome. This follows not from the nature of the thing but from their disease; and as the insane revile those who tend them, so do unbelievers, and those insulted should the more compassionate them and weep.

Calvin treats the first clause as a deliberate concession. Since it might readily be objected that the gospel is held in contempt when presented in so bare and abject a form, Paul grants it — but by naming whose estimate it is, he intimates that no regard need be paid to their judgment, for who would choose to despise the gospel at the expense of perishing? The prophecy he uses to the same end: it is unreasonable that the truth be held in prejudice because the wise of this world deride it, since in God's account their opinion is reckoned as nothing. Cyril of Jerusalem argues that we should glory in the Cross rather than be ashamed of it, since it was not a mere man who died for us but the Son of God made man; if the lamb under Moses drove the destroyer away, much more shall the Lamb of God deliver us — the blood of a silly sheep gave salvation, and shall not the Blood of the Only-begotten much rather save?

On the quotation they work as textual critics. Ellicott notes it joins two passages of Isaiah and follows the Greek version with one word altered, and that words originally aimed at those who assumed to guide the Jewish race apply with greater force to men who would presume to be Christian leaders. Gill sets the Hebrew beside the Greek: under the gospel the mysteries of grace are hidden from the wise rabbins, for all their sagacity and learning. Barnes judges the Hebrew sense not materially different, tracing the original to the iniquity of Jerusalem. Robertson identifies the setting as the failure of worldly statesmanship before the Assyrian invasion: there is such a thing as the ignorance of the learned and the wisdom of the simple-minded, and God's wisdom rises in the Cross sheer above a human philosophizing that is still scoffing at it. Clarke turns the verse against the sceptics, insisting that the really useful discoveries were made by men who feared God and credited divine revelation — Newton, Boyle, Pascal and others.
20:
Whether the triple question quotes the prophet at all is disputed. Calvin denies it flatly: Paul has not taken this from Isaiah, as is commonly thought, but speaks in his own person, the passage pointed to having nothing to do with the subject. Gill agrees they are the apostle's own words while allowing an allusion to phrases much like them whose meaning is very different, and adds that the Talmudists read those in a sense near his. Barnes takes the middle ground: without designing to quote the words as having any original reference here, Paul uses them as any man uses language he and his readers know, since one familiar with the Bible naturally speaks in its expressions. Robertson says he uses the passage without exact quotation; Ellicott calls it a quotation given general application, originally a song of triumph over Israel's enemies, and Wesley a bold and beautiful allusion.

Who the three are divides the same men. Clarke says the words most manifestly refer to the Jews, since the places alluded to can mean no others, and maps each term onto a Hebrew office — the wise onto the teacher, the scribe onto any learned man and especially a master of the traditions, the disputer onto the propounder of questions and seeker of allegorical meanings. John Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic source for the very sequence, a saying that God showed Adam every generation and its disputers, its wise men, its scribes and its governors, and glosses the terms the same way. Ellicott divides them by nation: the first refers to those who exalt human knowledge, the second to the Jew, the third to the Greek who discussed philosophy — and the qualifying phrase governs all three, not the last alone, the word meaning not the physical world but this age against the age to come. Robertson divides them the same way and notes the absence of the article in each question.

The harder phrase is the one about God's wisdom, and John Lightfoot turns it inside out: it means not the wisdom which had God for its author but the wisdom which had God for its object, and should be rendered wisdom about God — among the heathen there was a wisdom about natural things and a wisdom about God, that is, divinity, so that the world in its divinity could not by wisdom know God. Clarke reproduces that note under its author's name, the third such borrowing in this chapter. The others keep the wisdom God's own. Ellicott says it can scarcely express approval of God's arrangement of revelation but refers to his wisdom evidenced in nature and in the teaching of lawgivers and prophets. Barnes allows two interpretations and gives the first to the wisdom evinced in creation, so that the world surveying those works still did not know him. Gill canvasses Christ and the gospel before choosing creation. Wesley reads it as God's wise disposal in leaving them to make the trial, though the whole creation declared its Creator.

Calvin makes the failure a reversal. The right order was that man, contemplating the wisdom of God in his works by the light of nature, should arrive at an acquaintance with him; since depravity overturned that order, God designs first to make us see ourselves fools, and then, as a token of his wisdom, presents something wearing the appearance of folly — an inversion which the ingratitude of mankind deserved. Robertson calls the clause a solemn dirge of doom on both Greek philosophy and Jewish theology for failing to know God, then asks whether modern philosophy has done better and remarks that there is now even a godless theology. On the last phrase he presses a distinction the English hides: the word is not the act of heralding but the message proclaimed, so that what is called foolishness is the content and not the performance.
22:
The two demands are set out as national habits. Ellicott notes the Greek has neither article, so it is not the Jews and the Gentiles but Jewish-minded persons wanting visible portents and Greek-minded persons wanting a philosophic proof; the preaching pandered to neither. Barnes explains the first appetite historically: God had manifested himself to that people by miracles, and they prided themselves on it, demanding the same of any new messenger. Gill adds that though miracles were wrought such as never man did they remained incredulous; Clarke, that the plural reading is genuine and has been admitted into the text, no people being ever more difficult to persuade. Robertson borrows a neat antithesis, that the Jews claimed the truth while the Greeks were seekers; Wesley glosses the second appetite as the depths of philosophy and the charms of eloquence. Calvin observes that the apostle goes a step farther, since the Jews do not simply despise the gospel but abhor it.

Against both stands one sentence. Barnes puts the emphasis on the last word, since the Jews would have made their expected Messiah no less an object of glorying and spurned only the doctrine of a crucified one. Clarke explains the offence from the manner of the coming — meek, lowly and impoverished, where a mighty prince was expected. Wesley sets the two halves opposite the two demands, a stumbling-block opposite the signs and a silly tale opposite the wisdom, the preaching being plain and historical, not rhetorical. Robertson makes the same point of the verb, that they proclaim and do not dispute, presenting one who is neither a sign-shower nor a philosopher, and finds in the papyri that the word for the offence means a trap, which here tripped Jews wanting a conquering Messiah. Ellicott turns it round: the gospel made its way by the very qualities they counted weakness and folly, while Gill notes they preached a crucified Christ and him only.

Who the called are is the sharpest division here. Gill takes them as effectually called by grace, not merely externally but internally, so that being savingly illuminated they see beauty in Christ. Calvin makes the difference elective: the unfavourable reception was owing neither to any fault in Christ nor to the disposition of mankind generally, but to the depravity of those not enlightened by God, since the elect are hindered by nothing from coming to him. Clarke reads the word as invitation, of those called to the marriage feast who believed. Ellicott warns against the other way, that the apostle always speaks of all Christians as the called and never uses the word in the narrower sense to which some modern sects have restricted it. Wesley adds that they obey the heavenly calling; Robertson, that the answer is understood by open minds.

The closing comparison is guarded before it is made. Gill insists there is no foolishness in God nor the least weakness, the words being an ironical concession to what the world esteems such; Barnes says the passage does not affirm the thing is really unwise but that it appears so, and may point to parts of the divine administration where the plan's wisdom is concealed; Calvin repeats that this is a concession, since in strict propriety neither foolishness nor weakness can be ascribed to God. Then the grammarians part company over what the comparison is with. Ellicott holds it is not wiser than the wisdom of men, as some understand it, but wiser than men themselves, the word embracing all men can know or hope to know. Robertson gives exactly the reading Ellicott rejects, calling it a condensed comparison — wiser than the wisdom of men — a common Greek idiom which brushes all men aside; of the second half he says the Cross seemed God's defeat. Clarke and Wesley take the practical sense, that works appearing contemptible to superficial observers surpass all human power.
26:
The first word is ambiguous in form, and they handle it differently. Ellicott prefers the imperative, see your calling; Clarke the same, consider it. Robertson notes the form serves equally for indicative and imperative and that either makes sense. Calvin declines to settle it and leaves the choice to the reader, the meaning being the same either way: as a statement it summons them as witnesses of a thing manifest, as a command it stirs them up. Gill takes the noun for the men called by grace, as circumcision stands for the circumcised, while Robertson keeps it to the act of calling, resting not on their condition but on God's sovereign love.

What they are told to look at is a social fact. Clarke observes that the word men is not in the original and that the apostle means the Corinthian believers in particular, against the worldly notions of the Jews. Ellicott allows that a few of high birth were called, but not many, and quotes the remark that the ancient Christians were for the greater part slaves. Barnes states the argument plainly: the gospel did not depend for its success on human wisdom, those blessed by it not generally coming from the elevated ranks. Wesley glosses the terms as wise in the world's account, and men of power. Henry presses the qualification the other way, that not many is not none: God did not choose philosophers, orators, statesmen or men of wealth to publish the gospel, since he best judges what serves his glory, yet some noble in every age were not ashamed of it, and every rank needs pardoning grace.

The verbs of choosing are counted. Robertson notes the solemn verb occurs three times, each with its purpose stated — twice that God might put to shame, once that he might bring to naught — and that the aorist of the verb for boasting brings out sharply that not a single boast is to be made. Ellicott explains the shift of gender, the neuter generalising the qualities of the men chosen while the masculine of the wise shows persons are meant. Gill notes that the Jews called others the fools of the world, in distinction from their rabbins; Clarke, that by men esteemed rude and illiterate God confounded the greatest of the Greek philosophers.

The last term draws a textual and a national comment. Ellicott says the climax loses force through two intrusions — a connective absent from the best manuscripts and another word found in no manuscript at all — so that without them the phrase summarises rather than adds; Barnes says the insertion enfeebles the sense. Wesley and Clarke identify the phrase as Jewish contempt for the Gentiles, whom they held no better than dogs — and Clarke adds that by these very people, converted, God brought all the Jewish pretensions to nothing. Calvin distinguishes this nothingness from another: in Romans the same terms describe what we are before God, whereas here they concern only the opinion of men. On the closing purpose he says the word for flesh, though it denotes all mankind, carries a particular sting, the Spirit beating down human pride by speaking of it contemptuously — and that nothing is left us in which we may justly glory, though many delight for a moment in a false glorying which vanishes like smoke. Wesley calls it a fit appellation, fair but withering as grass; Gill lists what it excludes — blood, birth, lineage, dominion, riches, learning — gloried in before men but not before God; Clarke adds that though God employs men as instruments they have no part in the contrivance or the energy. Chrysostom sums the argument: human wisdom has been cast out two ways, by the testimony of the Scriptures and by the issue of events, and shown to be no new thing but foretold from the beginning.
30:
Where the emphasis falls is agreed. Barnes puts it on the two words saying what they are: Christians not by the agency of man but of God, owing their hopes to him and not to wealth or rank. Robertson reads the opening preposition as out of God — he chose you — the choice being made in the sphere of Christ, which is itself God's wisdom. Calvin calls the words emphatic: they have their beginning from God, who calls the things that are not and passes by those that appear to be, so that their subsistence is founded on Christ and they have no occasion to be proud; and this is not creation but the spiritual existence into which we are born again. Gill traces it further back, to a putting into Christ by electing grace without regard to merit, which he calls their original secret being in him, made manifest by regenerating grace. Ellicott states the consequence: so far from boasting in his presence, we owe all to him; Wesley glosses it as out of free grace, the state being engraftment into Christ.

The four titles are divided or subordinated. Robertson notices that the verb is became and not was, pointing to the Incarnation, Cross and Resurrection, and argues from the connectives that the three following words explain the first rather than adding to it. Ellicott takes the tense the same way — made, not is, referring to the Incarnation, in which Christ became God's revelation of himself and so a wisdom surpassing anything derived from nature or from man — but lists what follows as further gifts, adding righteousness and holiness to knowledge and then, beyond all that, redemption. Clarke defines each against a rival: the wisdom excels that of the philosopher and the scribe and even the constitution called the wisdom of the Jews; the righteousness is justification, procuring the remission the law could not give; the sanctification works in us not the external holiness that was the Jews' but a real one. Wesley defines each against a prior condition: wisdom for those before utterly foolish, righteousness for those before under wrath, sanctification for those before dead in sin, redemption as complete deliverance and eternal bliss.

The closing quotation is loosely made, and they say so. Barnes calls it a quotation not made literally, the prophet's sense condensed but retained; Ellicott, not a literal quotation but an adaptation and paraphrase of the Greek version. Robertson finds a probable ellipse of a kind common in these letters, and notes that some explain the imperative instead as a broken construction. Clarke sets out the prophet's words — that the wise not glory in his wisdom, the mighty in his might, the rich in his riches — and rules that whoever has any such thing should acknowledge he has nothing but what he received.

What the boast leaves standing is the last question. Calvin gives the sharpest answer: God does not despoil us to leave us bare but forthwith clothes us with his glory — on this condition, that whenever we would glory we go out of ourselves, so that a man brought to nothing in his own estimation renounces all desire for his own glory. Barnes draws inferences instead, that the plan of salvation is designed to exalt God and to humble us, and that all just views of the creation tend to produce true humility. Ellicott quotes an ancient remark that the apostle always fastens his readers on with nails to the name of Christ. Wesley states the negative side: not in himself, not in the flesh, not in the world. Robertson closes on the paragraph's value as evidence rather than doctrine, citing the judgement that what it shows about the origin of the congregations among the lower classes of the large towns makes it one of the most important historical witnesses to primitive Christianity.
